prompt: In the till's traceroute to `files`, what is hop 2, `10.20.0.1`?
hint: It is an address from the tunnel's own network.

choices.text: The ISP's router, answering from a private address
choices.why: The ISP carried encrypted UDP and never saw the traceroute's packets inside it.

choices.text: hq's address inside the tunnel
choices.why: Right. The whole crossing of the internet shows as that one hop.

choices.text: The branch router's public side
choices.why: branch is hop 1, answering from 192.168.20.1.

choices.text: The file server's second address
choices.why: files is hop 3, at 192.168.10.10.

prompt: Why does the ISP's router not appear at all in the till's traceroute?
hint: Whose TTL does the ISP decrement?

choices.text: It is set up never to answer a traceroute
choices.why: It never received an expired probe to answer; the probes were inside encrypted packets.

choices.text: ICMP rate limiting hid its hop
choices.why: Rate limiting leaves a star in the list; here there is no line for it at all.

choices.text: The probes crossed it inside encrypted packets
choices.why: Right. It decremented the outer header's TTL, never the probes'.

choices.text: The till has a route that goes straight to hq
choices.why: The till has a default route to branch and nothing else.

prompt: What in the till's own configuration tells it about the VPN?
hint: Its `ip route` had two lines.

choices.text: A route to 192.168.10.0/24 through wg0
choices.why: That route is on the routers; the till has no wg0.

choices.text: A WireGuard key pair of its own
choices.why: The keys are on branch, the router, not on the devices behind it.

choices.text: Nothing: a default route and its own LAN
choices.why: Right. It would look the same over a leased line.

choices.text: An address from the tunnel's 10.20.0.0/24
choices.why: Only the routers and remote have tunnel addresses.

prompt: A visitor plugs a laptop into the branch LAN. With the lab set up as it is, what can it reach at the head office?
hint: What does this tunnel authenticate?

choices.text: The same as any machine on that network
choices.why: Right. The tunnel authenticates a site, and the visitor is now part of it; firewall rules and a guest VLAN are the answer.

choices.text: Nothing, since it holds no WireGuard key
choices.why: The key is the branch router's, and it carries the visitor's packets like anyone else's.

choices.text: Only hq's tunnel address, 10.20.0.1
choices.why: hq's AllowedIPs for branch includes the whole branch LAN.

choices.text: The head office, after a login with MFA
choices.why: A site-to-site tunnel has no login at all.

prompt: What does a remote-access connection authenticate that a site-to-site tunnel does not?
hint: Lesson 4's status file wrote one word beside the address.

choices.text: The public address the laptop connects from
choices.why: It changes between home and a hotel, and proves nothing about who is there.

choices.text: A person, and ideally the device
choices.why: Right. `ana` in the status file is a person's certificate.

choices.text: The home router doing the NAT
choices.why: Nobody authenticates homegw; it only forwards her packets.

choices.text: The branch office's router
choices.why: That is what a site-to-site tunnel authenticates.

prompt: Why do companies ask for MFA on a remote-access VPN, on top of a password?
hint: What does one successful login give away?

choices.text: WireGuard refuses connections without a second factor
choices.why: WireGuard knows nothing of MFA; the lab used keys alone.

choices.text: A second factor makes the tunnel's encryption stronger
choices.why: The encryption is the same either way; MFA is about who logs in.

choices.text: One stolen password would put an attacker inside the network
choices.why: Right. The gateway faces the internet, and behind it is everything the pool reaches.

choices.text: The law requires it of every VPN
choices.why: The reason is the risk of a door facing the internet, not a universal rule.

prompt: Ten people share one WireGuard key and one peer entry on the concentrator. One of them leaves the company. What is the problem?
hint: What would the concentrator have to stop accepting?

choices.text: Her AllowedIPs can be removed and the rest stay
choices.why: There is one peer entry and one AllowedIPs for all ten.

choices.text: hq has to delete the key from her laptop remotely
choices.why: The office cannot reach into her laptop; it can only stop accepting the key.

choices.text: Cutting her off means a new key for all ten
choices.why: Right. And no log ever said which of the ten was connected, since they were one peer.

choices.text: The pool runs out of addresses
choices.why: Ten people is nothing to a /24, and they share one address anyway.

prompt: Match each description to the end of a VPN it belongs to.
hint: Two are site to site, two are remote access.

pairs.left: Up at three in the morning with nobody logged in
pairs.right: A tunnel between two office routers

pairs.left: Its far end moves between home and a hotel
pairs.right: A client on a laptop, behind somebody's NAT

pairs.left: Carries the tills, which could never run a client
pairs.right: The branch router, on their behalf

pairs.left: Writes one name per connection in its status file
pairs.right: A concentrator with a certificate per person

right_distractors: The ISP's router, which reads inside the tunnel

prompt: With the split tunnel, which way did Ana's request to `web1` go?
hint: `ip route get 192.0.2.21` answered before the traceroute did.

choices.text: Through wg0 to hq, and out from there
choices.why: That is the full tunnel; split, web1 is not in AllowedIPs.

choices.text: Out of eth0, through her home router
choices.why: Right. via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0, and the traceroute went homegw, ISP, web1.

choices.text: Through wg0 to branch
choices.why: branch is not one of Ana's peers.

choices.text: Nowhere, because web1 could not be reached
choices.why: curl printed served by web1.

prompt: `web1`'s log shows `198.51.100.77` for Ana's split request and `203.0.113.2` for her full one. Why the second address?
hint: Whose address is 203.0.113.2?

choices.text: Her home router got a new public address
choices.why: homegw is still 198.51.100.77; 203.0.113.2 is hq's.

choices.text: web1 logs the tunnel's address instead of the client's
choices.why: Her tunnel address is 10.20.0.3, which web1 never saw.

choices.text: hq sent it out and translated it to its own address
choices.why: Right. The full tunnel ends at hq, and hq's NAT makes her traffic look like the office's.

choices.text: The ISP rewrote the source on the way
choices.why: The ISP routes; the rewriting happened at hq.

prompt: With `AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0`, why does `wg-quick` mark WireGuard's own packets with `fwmark 51820`?
hint: Where would the encrypted UDP to hq go under a default route through wg0?

choices.text: To give the tunnel's traffic priority on the uplink
choices.why: A mark here chooses a routing table, not a queue.

choices.text: So that hq can tell which peer is sending
choices.why: A mark never leaves the machine; hq tells peers apart by key.

choices.text: So that the firewall can count the tunnel's bytes
choices.why: wg show counts them already; the mark exists for routing.

choices.text: So the encrypted packets avoid table 51820
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the tunnel's own packets would be routed back into the tunnel.

prompt: `ip route get` asks the kernel which way a packet would go, without ___ one.
hint: It is a question, not a test.

prompt: Which of these are reasons to choose a full tunnel? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of what hq sees, and what hq carries.

choices.text: The company's filtering and logs apply to all her traffic
choices.why: Right: everything leaves through hq.

choices.text: Her video calls get faster
choices.why: They take a detour, crossing the head office's link twice.

choices.text: Services that accept only the office's address work from home
choices.why: Right: web1 saw 203.0.113.2.

choices.text: The head office's uplink carries less
choices.why: It carries more: all of her traffic, in and out.

choices.text: On a café's Wi-Fi her traffic crosses the local network encrypted
choices.why: Right, as long as her DNS goes the same way.

prompt: In the full tunnel, how many times does Ana's request to `web1` pass through the ISP's router?
hint: Once on the way to hq, encrypted.

prompt: Split tunnel, no DNS setting: Ana looks up a name that only the company's DNS server knows. What happens?
hint: Which resolver does her laptop ask?

choices.text: The query goes through wg0 because the name is internal
choices.why: Routes decide by address, and the resolver she asks is on the home LAN.

choices.text: WireGuard answers it from hq's configuration
choices.why: WireGuard knows nothing about names.

choices.text: The home router's resolver has never heard of it
choices.why: Right. It fails, which is what split DNS fixes.

choices.text: It resolves, since DNS always travels in the tunnel
choices.why: Nothing sends DNS through the tunnel unless a resolver on the company side is set.

prompt: Ana's full tunnel is up, and her resolver is still the home router, `192.168.1.1`. Where do her DNS queries go?
hint: Which rule keeps the home LAN reachable?

choices.text: Through wg0 to hq, like everything else
choices.why: suppress_prefixlength 0 lets the main table's route for the home LAN win.

choices.text: Across her home LAN in clear, bypassing wg0
choices.why: Right. A DNS leak: the names she looks up cross the home network in clear.

choices.text: Nowhere, because the full tunnel blocks the LAN
choices.why: The LAN stays reachable on purpose.

choices.text: To the ISP's resolver, by way of hq
choices.why: hq only sees what enters wg0, and these queries never do.

prompt: After `RTNETLINK answers: File exists`, what state was Ana's tunnel left in?
hint: Read the last line wg-quick printed.

choices.text: Up, without the one colliding route
choices.why: wg-quick treats the failure as fatal.

choices.text: Up, with the home LAN now through wg0
choices.why: The kernel refused the route; eth0 kept the home LAN.

choices.text: Gone: wg-quick deleted wg0
choices.why: Right. ip link delete dev wg0 undid everything, the route to 192.168.10.0/24 included.

choices.text: Up, but only for the tunnel's own 10.20.0.0/24
choices.why: No wg0 was left to carry anything.

prompt: Put in order what `wg-quick` did when the home range was added to `AllowedIPs`.
hint: The address comes before the routes.
trap: The failure came after the office route was already in, and the deletion took that route away too.

prompt: A contractor needs one web application and nothing else on the network. What fits best?
hint: How much of the network does each option expose?

choices.text: A remote-access VPN account with a full tunnel
choices.why: It reaches every address the pool allows, far more than one application.

choices.text: Per-application access through a broker
choices.why: Right. The session reaches that application and nothing else.

choices.text: A site-to-site tunnel to the contractor's office
choices.why: That joins their whole office to your network.

choices.text: The application's port opened to the internet
choices.why: That exposes it to everybody, not to one contractor.

prompt: Why can per-application access not replace the tunnel between `hq` and `branch`?
hint: Who, or what, would the broker check?

choices.text: It does not work across the internet
choices.why: Working across the internet is its whole design.

choices.text: The branch has no public address for it
choices.why: branch has 198.51.100.2.

choices.text: The tills there have no person to check
choices.why: Right. It checks a person and a device per application; a till is neither a person nor able to run the client.

choices.text: It cannot encrypt what it carries
choices.why: The broker's connections are encrypted too.

prompt: A head office LAN is `192.168.0.0/24`, and half the staff have home routers on the same range. Which fix causes the fewest surprises later?
hint: Which side does the company control?

choices.text: Ask the staff to renumber their home routers
choices.why: Dozens of networks you do not run, and every new hire starts again.

choices.text: Add 192.168.0.0/24 to every laptop's AllowedIPs anyway
choices.why: wg-quick stops with File exists, as the capture showed.

choices.text: Use a full tunnel so that the office range wins
choices.why: suppress_prefixlength 0 keeps the home LAN's route in charge.

choices.text: Renumber the company side to a rare block
choices.why: Right. One renumbering the company controls, instead of a collision in every home.

prompt: A clinic's reception PCs at two sites use the same patient system at the head office all day. What do you build?
hint: Is the traffic a person's or a site's?

choices.text: A tunnel between each site's router and the head office
choices.why: Right. Always up, invisible to the PCs, and one configuration per site.

choices.text: A remote-access client on every reception PC
choices.why: It works, at the cost of a client and a login per PC for traffic that is really the site's.

choices.text: A split tunnel on the receptionists' phones
choices.why: The phones are not what needs the system.

choices.text: The patient system published on the internet
choices.why: That exposes patient records to anybody who finds it.
